lesson.title: Catching Mistakes: How the Cell Proofreads and Repairs Its Own DNA
lesson.summary: DNA polymerase corrects most of its own errors on the spot using a built-in proofreading activity, and separate mismatch repair systems catch nearly everything that slips through, keeping the overall mutation rate extraordinarily low.
lesson.body:
DNA polymerase is astonishingly accurate, but it is not perfect. Occasionally, during the synthesis described in the DNA Polymerase chapter, the enzyme inserts the wrong nucleotide, for instance pairing a G opposite a template T instead of the correct A. If left uncorrected, this kind of mistake becomes a permanent change to the DNA sequence, a mutation, that gets copied again in every future round of replication.

Fortunately, many DNA polymerases have a built-in safeguard: a proofreading activity, carried out by a separate part of the same enzyme that acts as a 3' to 5' exonuclease. After adding each new nucleotide, the polymerase effectively checks whether it paired correctly with the template. A mismatched base pair distorts the normal geometry of the double helix just enough for the enzyme to sense that something is wrong. When that happens, the polymerase backs up, uses its exonuclease activity to clip out the incorrect nucleotide, and then tries again with the correct one before continuing synthesis forward. This proofreading happens essentially in real time, as part of the same replication process described throughout this unit.

Proofreading catches most errors immediately, but not every mistake is caught in the act. A second line of defense, called mismatch repair, scans newly replicated DNA after the fact for base pairs that still do not match up correctly. These repair systems are able to tell which of the two strands is the original template and which is the newly synthesized strand, so they know which strand contains the error that needs fixing rather than accidentally changing the correct original sequence. The mismatched segment on the new strand is cut out and resynthesized correctly.

Together, proofreading during synthesis and mismatch repair afterward make DNA replication remarkably faithful, with only a tiny fraction of errors ultimately surviving as permanent mutations. This matters beyond just accuracy for its own sake: when the genes that encode these repair systems themselves stop working properly, mutations accumulate much faster than normal, and this loss of repair capacity is linked to an increased risk of certain cancers. Proofreading and repair are a good reminder that DNA polymerase's job is not simply to add nucleotides quickly, it is to add the correct nucleotides, and to catch itself when it does not.
